problems.title: Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. How many distinct ways can you climb to the top?
problems.understanding: At every step, you can climb either 1 or 2 stairs. To reach step n, you come from n-1 or n-2.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Generate every climb step combination by recursively deciding whether to take 1 or 2 steps.

problems.intuition: Subproblem overlap means dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]. We can build bottom-up or optimize space to only 2 variables.
problems.approach:
1. Check base cases: if n <= 2, return n.
  2. Maintain prev2 = 1 and prev1 = 2.
  3. Loop from 3 to n updating current = prev1 + prev2, shifting prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = current.
  4. Return prev1.
problems.takeaway: Previous 2 states DP — Each state only depends on the immediate two previous states.

problems.title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
problems.statement: Given an integer array cost where cost[i] is the cost of i-th step on a staircase. Once you pay the cost, you can climb 1 or 2 steps. Return the minimum cost to reach the top of the floor.
problems.understanding: You can start from step 0 or step 1. At step i, cost incurred to jump is cost[i] + min(cost_of_next_1, cost_of_next_2).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Recursively try starting from 0 and 1, taking min cost of jumping 1 or 2 steps at each index.

problems.intuition: Building bottom-up: dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]). Can be space-optimized to two variables.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize prev2 = 0 and prev1 = 0.
  2. Loop i from 2 to len(cost).
  3. current = min(prev1 + cost[i-1], prev2 + cost[i-2]).
  4. Shift prev2 = prev1, prev1 = current. Return prev1.
problems.takeaway: Minimum previous states DP — Transition depends on minimum of previous subproblem choices.

problems.title: House Robber
problems.statement: You are a professional robber planning to rob houses along a street. Each house has a certain amount of money stashed. Adjacent houses have security systems connected, so you cannot rob two adjacent houses. Return maximum money you can rob.
problems.understanding: At every house: Rob it (gain nums[i] + profit from house i-2) OR skip it (keep profit from house i-1).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Explore all choices at each house recursively.

problems.intuition: State equation: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], nums[i] + dp[i-2]). We can optimize space by keeping only prev1 and prev2.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize prev2 = 0 and prev1 = 0.
  2. Iterate through money in nums.
  3. Compute current = max(prev1, money + prev2).
  4. Update prev2 = prev1 and prev1 = current. Return prev1.
problems.takeaway: Take / Skip DP — Classic binary choice pattern at each element.

problems.title: House Robber II
problems.statement: Houses form a circle, so the first and last houses are neighbors and cannot both be robbed. Return maximum money you can rob.
problems.understanding: Circular constraint means we split into two linear subproblems: Case 1 (houses 0 ... n-2) and Case 2 (houses 1 ... n-1). Return max of both.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Try all subsets while tracking whether the first house was robbed and previous house was robbed.

problems.intuition: Circular DP reduces to running House Robber I helper on two slices: nums[:-1] and nums[1:].
problems.approach:
1. If len(nums) == 1, return nums[0].
  2. Define linear rob helper function rob_linear(arr) using space-optimized House Robber I logic.
  3. Return max(rob_linear(nums[:-1]), rob_linear(nums[1:])).
problems.takeaway: Circular DP → split into two linear DP problems.

problems.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the longest palindromic substring in s.
problems.understanding: A palindrome expands outward from its center. There are odd-length centers (single char) and even-length centers (between two chars).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Check every substring s[i:j+1] to see if it is a palindrome.

problems.intuition: Expand outwards from each center index i (odd) and pair (i, i+1) (even) as long as characters match.
problems.approach:
1. Helper expand(left, right) expands outward while s[left] == s[right].
  2. For each index i, compute odd palindrome bounds expand(i, i) and even palindrome bounds expand(i, i+1).
  3. Keep track of maximum length slice bounds start, end and return s[start:end+1].
problems.takeaway: Expand Around Center — Palindrome expansion technique beats standard O(n²) 2D DP in auxiliary space.

problems.title: Palindromic Substrings
problems.statement: Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it.
problems.understanding: Every palindrome expands outward around a center. Single characters and pairs of characters serve as centers.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Check every substring to see if it is a palindrome.

problems.intuition: Expand outward from each index i (odd) and pair (i, i+1) (even), incrementing count for each matching expansion.
problems.approach:
1. Helper expand(left, right) increments count while s[left] == s[right].
  2. For each index i, call expand(i, i) and expand(i, i+1).
  3. Return total count.

problems.title: Decode Ways
problems.statement: A message containing letters A-Z is encoded using 1-26. Return total number of ways to decode string s.
problems.understanding: Try decoding one digit (if non-zero) or two digits (if between 10 and 26). 1 or 2 character state transitions.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Recursively try single digit and double digit decodings from index i.

problems.intuition: dp[i] stores number of ways to decode string of length i. Optimize space to prev1 and prev2.
problems.approach:
1. If empty string or starts with '0', return 0.
  2. Maintain prev2 = 1 and prev1 = 1.
  3. For index i from 1 to len(s)-1: if s[i] != '0', current += prev1. If 10 <= int(s[i-1:i+1]) <= 26, current += prev2.
  4. Shift prev2 = prev1, prev1 = current. Return prev1.

problems.title: Coin Change
problems.statement: Given coin denominations and amount, return fewest coins needed to make up amount. If impossible return -1.
problems.understanding: Unbounded choice + minimum coins → 1-D DP array where dp[i] = min(dp[i], 1 + dp[i - coin]).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Try every coin denomination recursively at each remaining target amount.

problems.intuition: Initialize dp array of size amount + 1 with infinity (or amount + 1) and dp[0] = 0. Fill from 1 to amount.
problems.approach:
1. Create dp = [amount + 1] * (amount + 1), set dp[0] = 0.
  2. For current from 1 to amount: for each coin in coins: if coin <= current, update dp[current] = min(dp[current], dp[current - coin] + 1).
  3. Return dp[amount] if dp[amount] <= amount else -1.

problems.title: Maximum Product Subarray
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums, find contiguous non-empty subarray that has largest product.
problems.understanding: Multiplying a negative number by the smallest negative product can turn it into the largest positive product. Thus, track BOTH max and min products.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Brute Force
naive.html: Calculate product of every subarray using nested loops.

problems.intuition: Track current_max and current_min. When num < 0, swap current_max and current_min before updating.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize current_max = nums[0], current_min = nums[0], answer = nums[0].
  2. For num in nums[1:]: if num < 0, swap current_max, current_min.
  3. Update current_max = max(num, current_max * num) and current_min = min(num, current_min * num).
  4. Update answer = max(answer, current_max). Return answer.
problems.takeaway: When the operation can flip states, track both max and min.

problems.title: Word Break
problems.statement: Given string s and dictionary wordDict, return true if s can be segmented into words from dictionary.
problems.understanding: Prefix DP: dp[i] is True if prefix s[:i] can be segmented into dictionary words.
problems.intuition: Use boolean array dp of size n+1 with dp[0] = True. For each index i, check if dp[j] == True and s[j:i] is in words.
problems.approach:
1. Convert wordDict to a set words.
  2. Initialize dp = [False] * (n + 1) and dp[0] = True.
  3. Loop i from 1 to n, and j from 0 to i-1. If dp[j] and s[j:i] in words, set dp[i] = True and break.
  4. Return dp[n].

problems.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.statement: Given an integer array nums, return length of longest strictly increasing subsequence.
problems.understanding: At each element, we can take it (if larger than previous taken element) or skip it. Standard DP is O(n²), patience sort / binary search optimizes to O(n log n).

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Try taking or skipping every element recursively.

problems.intuition: O(n²) DP: dp[i] represents length of LIS ending at index i. Binary Search: tails array tracks smallest tail of all increasing subsequences.
problems.approach:
1. Initialize empty list tails.
  2. For each num in nums: binary search target index in tails using bisect_left.
  3. If index equals len(tails), append num. Else overwrite tails[index] = num.
  4. Return len(tails).

optimal.title: Optimized Code (Python 3)
complexity: Time: O(n log n) (Binary Search) / O(n²) (Standard DP)

problems.takeaway: LIS → DP first, then recognize the patience-sorting/binary-search optimization.

problems.title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.statement: Given integer array nums, return true if array can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sum.
problems.understanding: If sum(nums) is odd, partition is impossible. Target sum is total // 2. This is a classic 0/1 Knapsack problem.

naive.title: Naive Solution — Recursion
naive.html: Try putting every number into either subset recursively.

problems.intuition: Boolean array dp[c] stores whether target sum c is reachable. Loop backwards to use each number at most once!
problems.approach:
1. Compute total = sum(nums). If total % 2, return False. target = total // 2.
  2. Initialize dp = [False] * (target + 1) with dp[0] = True.
  3. For num in nums: loop current backward from target down to num: dp[current] = dp[current] or dp[current - num].
  4. Return dp[target].
problems.takeaway: 0/1 Knapsack Backward Loop — Loop backward (range(target, num - 1, -1)) so each number is used only once.
